utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably before we proceed, probably we need some clarification from the Prosecution about the format of F11. The main schedule refers to the only wound, while the footnote says evidence shows there is a dead man. Let me be precise. Yes, the footnote says: "The evidence also shows that one person was killed." And there's an additional nine wounded. What does it mean? Mr. Tieger, are you in the position to answer the question? What was alleged by the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, you caught me in the middle of something else, but let me consult with Ms. Edgerton. I'm not entirely sure it bears on -- precisely on -- or is dispositive to the issue raised here, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I will consult with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you need to think about it, while we will allow the accused to continue. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how, given these facts, the shooting from incident 11 and the physical evidence, what do -- does that point to?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All physical evidence indicates that fire was opened from the building of the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I may finish, the victim mentioned here - and the entry and exit wounds of that victim were described in the official report - indicate that the projectile hit the body from under a great angle of descent. While we were working on this, we didn't have a good-quality photograph, but we saw such a photograph for the first time later. It was not available to us. The official report states that he was hit by a bullet under a great angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded that the projectile may have come from the Executive Council and that Edin Suljic confirmed that the angle of descent was very great, Edin Suljic, in February this year in the Mladic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger will --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, either one of us are prepared to quickly respond to the Court's inquiry. It happened that I was on my feet and then it was difficult to see at this angle. If I understand the Court's inquiry correctly, it's confirming what I think is fairly clear from the language of the indictment and the footnote, and that is that the -- what is charged here are the injuries to the victim named in -- in the scheduled incident. There's also a notation in the footnote that others were wounded or killed at the same time. They are not charged in this indictment. And that's -- but for whatever purposes of clarity may be served at any given time by that additional information, it was included. But the charged incident is identified in its totality in the body of the indictment under scheduled incident 11, not in the footnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Excellencies, in our system this would be called concealing or distortion. We are fully authorised to know everything that was a consequence of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me respond to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just let's stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and leave it there. Having heard the clarification, I take -- I find your comment very inappropriate, Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "in our system." Now let's see 1D7474. I don't understand the criteria of selection of victims from the same incident, why only one victim was selected and only one injured person, although there were several victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know you don't want an argument on this and I don't intend to enter into it. But if Mr. Karadzic will continue to try to provoke a response, I will rise and offer the opportunity for a response if the Court wishes. I think he should desist or he's going to hear more than he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is not a time for submissions. Please focus on your examination-in-chief of Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, can you help us with what you have stated? It's -- can we please see page 8790. This is 8716. This is further away. Now let us focus on line 18. I'll read out in English. [In English] "Mr. Ivetic: If we can look" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, now we have a part of the evidence of Mr. Suljic before this Chamber that Dr. Karadzic is going to proceed to read in, and I think this frankly needs to stop. And if Dr. Karadzic wants to call Edin Suljic as a witness in his Defence case, he can take the appropriate steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What did you mean by "we have a part of the evidence of Mr. Suljic before this Chamber"?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is what -- this is what we see on the screen now is the transcript of Mr. Suljic's evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the Mladic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- in the Mladic case that Dr. Karadzic is proceeding to read in before this Chamber, and I don't think that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If Dr. Karadzic wants to ask a question based on some assertion that Mr. Suljic may or may not have made, a hypothetical question, that's perfectly permissible, of course, Your Honours, but it's not the situation where he should be reading in the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I'm struck at how often Ms. Edgerton is objecting to things that the Prosecution itself has been doing with its own experts. There's information which is presented to its experts which does not have to be admissible - witness statements, videos, things like that - and the expert can take all of that information and use it in making their conclusion. And then when they're being asked in the full transparency that is required of experts, they can tell why they relied on and made certain conclusions and why they didn't. Now, that's what Mr. Poparic is doing here. He's saying what conclusion he drew and he's explaining why, and it's based on information that came in this case, in the evidence from the Mladic case. We're not offering this transcript. We're simply using it as a basis of showing why the expert reached a particular conclusion that he did. And there's nothing different that we're doing than the Prosecution did with its experts when they presented material to them for their review and when they tried to justify the conclusions that they reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From line 18 on this page till line 16 on the next, does this contain what you mentioned about the great angle of descent? He says in his answer --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see this here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I get the following page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I apologise. I was looking at the wrong side. Can this be enlarged? This is hard to read. Yes. It starts in line 12. Yes. That's the part where Mr. Suljic confirmed based on the photograph that this was fired at a great angle of descent. Maybe I can explain the situation. I said that in the official report there was a description of this wound, that the entry wound was on the right side of the face and the exit wound at the left shoulder-blade. Such a description of the wound indicates a great angle of descent of the projectile, which rules out the option that it was fired from the Metaljka building, as was alleged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this evidence confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even without all the evidence that we found, this would suffice to show that it was fired from the Executive Council building. I said that I didn't include this in my report because I didn't have a good-quality photograph at my disposal to conclude for myself that the police report was accurate. I saw that photograph for the first time at General Mladic's trial. There were other images shown there too which we didn't have, such as a design of the -- a blueprint of the design of the tram. But certainly this photograph matches the description in the official report and that confirms that the projectile was fired from a high altitude and came in at a great angle of descent. The only possible source was the Executive Council building, and that tallies with our conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was that photograph made and that design of the tram?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was made during the on-site investigation. It's police material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Just one matter, I mean that assumption is predicated on the basis that the victim was in a vertical or near-vertical position at the time of the impact of the round. If he had, for instance, been leaning over at the time of the impact of the round, that assumption wouldn't stand, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. If he was leaning over, that can be called into question. But the other evidence led also shows that the angle of descent was great and that the fire originated from the Executive Council building. The tram was near that building.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence can only be sorry that it did not have that design of the tram and that other evidence while the -- during the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you say at the end?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender the report 1D5600. It will be useful for the Chamber, and as for probative value that's for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is 1D5600? The inconsistency report? Yes, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3644, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for Mr. Poparic at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you begin, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I will indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, can I invite you to keep your answers as concise as you possibly can. First of all, is it correct that you have no formal training in criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You have no formal training in forensic pathology?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I'm not a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You have never worked as a sniper?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say here that my military specialty was not sniping, but I do have training in the use of infantry weapons. I was a professional military officer and we did have annual training with infantry weapons, various rifles, pistols, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You never served as a sniper in a combat environment; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never fought in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You have never been a sniper instructor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never been one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you have with Zorica Subotic and others co-authored five reports which have been presented to this Trial Chamber. Do you stand by the conclusions in all of those reports?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see Mrs. Subotic when she recently testified in this trial, by which I mean did you follow her testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you speak to her after she testified?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she went back home. I mean, we spoke briefly, we saw each other briefly, but we did not have an opportunity to sit down and discuss things in great detail. We just met here because the plan was that she would testify for a shorter period of time and that I would testify after her, and somehow it got longer. And then I stayed on and then she went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: For how long did you discuss her testimony with her?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say. How long? Say an hour. We didn't discuss the testimony for very long. We discussed other things too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up the modified air bombs report which has been admitted as D3540. This you co-authored with Mrs. Subotic, and if we could go, please --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- to page 209 in the B/C/S, page 214 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registrar to zoom in on the bottom right-hand corner of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The bottom right-hand corner, I think it's fair to say that this part of this map was not authored by you, but it says there: "If, following the model for the combat disposition of this 102nd Motorised Brigade, the positions of the other brigades of the 1st Corps of the BH army in the city were to be marked on a map showing the disposition of both sides, it would provide a realistic picture of Sarajevo as one more or less single large military target ..." Do you share that view?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my text. We used the text of General Radinovic who is a military expert, and we just used this as a guide-line in terms of the deployment of military units in the city of Sarajevo. We did not deal with that at all, whether Sarajevo was a military target. That was not the subject of our paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right. My --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you were to ask me personally, I don't think it was the entire city. If you're asking me as an officer, it's just the area where the army is and where fire is being opened from. That can be considered a military target, not the entire city, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to the question of the accuracy of modified air bombs used to target Sarajevo, and I'd like to turn to page 181 in B/C/S and 188 in English. On the page previous to this when you're introducing this data, you say that when estimating probable deviations in terms of direction, distance, and probable cruising deviation, it was assumed that the average range of bombs was 6.000 metres. So I take it that the dispersion data specifically in columns 6 and 7 is on the assumption that the modified air bombs were launched from 6.000 metres away from the target; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This is on the assumption where the target roughly was on the basis of the claims made. If it were 6.000, then it would all be the same; right? So probably it depends on the distance from which the fire is coming and it differs for each and every range, doesn't it? So ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. Transcript. The witness did not say "probably it depends." It was a different syntax. He said "probably the dispersion depends," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course all of these values are tentative because no one can establish exactly the position from where the firing came, so this is tentative. 500 metres, a kilometre more, it doesn't matter. These -- the dispersion data is basically there. That is the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Just one thing. It should be stated this way: "the probable dispersion." [In English] That is one syntax, "the probable dispersion."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, in this report you have indicated a Vd for every one of these air bombs of 43 metres, you have indicated a Vp of 77 metres for the FAB-250, and a Vp of 98 metres for the FAB-100 in each and every one of these incidents. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'll explain this to you. This is practically a rocket, a rocketised projectile. We are saying that these are modified bombs, but actually it's a rocket. In the case of rocket projectiles there is a characteristic in terms of the probable deviation that differs from classical projectiles, and dispersion is much bigger at shorter range than at longer range. And the dispersion in terms of direction is smaller, at smaller ranges, and it grows at longer ranges. This is a bit the other way around in terms of what is characteristic of classical projectiles. So then the results turned out to be more or less the same. These are approximations, perhaps not in terms of the decimal point; however, there is greater deviation in terms of direction because that is the characteristic of these rocket projectiles. This is a general characteristic because the dispersion increases with the increase of the range, and at first glance this may seem illogical but that is the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to the previous page in both languages, please. I want to clarify the data that you've given here. Now, if you take the opportunity to read to yourself paragraph 151, it's quite clear that the data is presented on the assumption that the projectile is fired from a distance of 6.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps the Registrar could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, before we broke I asked you to re-read paragraph 151 of the modified air bombs report. And can you now confirm that on the basis of that paragraph the table reproduces data on the assumption that the projectile was fired from a distance of 6.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. May I look at the table? Because I -- well, perhaps I didn't see it well, but it's in the text and probably that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if we turn to the table -- and we're all laypersons in this room, so in a moment we're going to get to the meaning of the terms "Vd" and "Vp." But for the moment can I confirm that it is your position that if you fire a FAB-250 from a distance 6.000 metres from the target, the Vd is 43 metres and the Vp is 77 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just an additional explanation because I can see it better now. These are different bombs here. This Vd and Vp was obtained on the assumption based on a mathematical model of an air bomb, and we gave these results and some diagrams, but in -- I mean in one report. But that text was redacted; that's why we don't have it. According to these results, in the case of all of these bombs, the Vd is the same. You know, the Vp varies. So if we look at the table, depending on the bomb, then the Vp is different. So basically I confirm what you said a moment ago so is this -- actually, I can explain why 6 was taken [as interpreted]. We just had to take one distance in order to be able to compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. And it's also clear from this table that if you fire a FAB-100 from a distance 6.000 metres from the target, the Vd is 43 metres and the Vp is 98 metres, according to your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we'll get to the lexicon which explains the terms in a minute, but translating that into layman's terms, it's correct, isn't it, that you're saying that if you fire a FAB-100 6 kilometres away from the target, there is a 50 per cent chance of it landing in an elliptical area of 196 metres by 86 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be more correct to say that it will fall plus/minus 98 in relation to the point because you do have this point in the sight and there is a deviation to the left/right, up and down. So that would be correct to put it that way. The physicality is different, although it is the ellipse that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the ellipse if you were to fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 25 on 58 page should be "6.000 was taken."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And translating your evidence in respect of the FAB-250, you're saying that there is a 50 per cent chance that a FAB-250 fired 6 kilometres away from the target would land in an elliptical area of 154 metres by 86 metres; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, to help those of us who do not have your level of military knowledge, can we call up please 65 ter 18915A. What's coming up, if we go to page 2 in the original and page 2 of the English, is a military lexicon published in Belgrade in 1981.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you kindly repeat the number, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. It's 18915A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like you just briefly to confirm that Vd is a dispersion of hits according to distance and Vp is a dispersion of hits according to direction and probable deviation is a measure of the dispersion of hits whose value in metres is chosen so that it is equally probable that half the hits are less than and the other half greater than this value.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not understand. I did not understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you just explain very briefly in layman's terms, what does Vd mean and what does Vp mean in the table that you've presented?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irrespective of the table, the very concept is not linked to the table. Some values are provided here that show the Vd and the Vp. Vd is the range error probable. That definition in itself shows that it is a statistical thing. It is probable dispersion. It shows what the deviation will be in relation to the sighting point. So that is the statistical deviation from that point. How does one obtain this Vd? This Vd is obtained --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. We don't need to look into that right now. I'll call up the lexicon. It's 18715A, please. We see on the next page that this was published in Belgrade in 1981 by the military publishing house. And if we go to the next page, could you please direct your eye to the entry for probable deviation, the next page in the B/C/S, please. It's at the top left, if we could zoom in on the top left entry. And we see there a description of Vd and Vp, and in particular they give an example further down where they say: "For example, the information for a mortar Vd equals 5 metres." It says that: "Half of all shots lie within the range plus or minus 5 metres around the mean impact point, while the other half deviate (diverge) by more than 5 metres."

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what I said a moment ago if we understood each other correctly. So in 1 Vd we have 50 per cent of hits. Just to be clear, that is one of the main characteristics of all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness start answering again, speaking slower and more clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you start again speaking more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wished to say that probable dispersion is one of the characteristics of all projectiles that is provided in firing tables, and it helps a user know roughly what the probability is of hitting the target. With 1 Vd probable dispersion we have 50 per cent and, for example, with 3 plus/minus Vd we have 97.5 per cent, so that is almost a certain hit. That is the practical importance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. And in your table you appear to be referring to 1 Vd, correct, where you say "Vd" in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Now we're going to turn to the very same analysis for the 122-millimetre Grad rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I tender this, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6346, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, at page 3 of your report you've confirmed, Mr. Poparic, that you participated in the development of the 122-millimetre Grad rocket during your career at Pretis.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just say that I took part in the initial stage. Later on I moved to other work. I know Grad and Oganj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very good. Now, it's true that Grad is just a nickname. The correct or more formal name for the Grad 122-millimetre is the M-21-OF?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can put it that way. The calibre is 122 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to look at the firing table in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I please ask the Registrar for 65 ter 24036, and if we go to page 12 in B/C/S, page 12 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I think if we just take the B/C/S, please, if we turn it up the right way you can see from the header of this, Mr. Poparic, that this is the firing table for the M-21-OF when it is used without a spoiler; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to look at the values, please, for when it is fired from 6.000 metres, and I believe we can see that when it is fired from 6.000 metres the Vd is 202 metres and the Vp is 34 metres. Could you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. It's a bit small. The print seems very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could focus on the left-hand side of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the names in the columns? That's how I can follow. The first line there. Now I found the column. Now it can be moved up. Actually -- yes, can you go ... You said 6.000 metres, 202, and 34; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone, and could all other microphones be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. You've confirmed what I said to you; is that correct, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what you said, but there is 202 and 34. Those are the two possible deviations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, the deviation by distance is 202 metres. The deviation by direction is 34 metres; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So essentially if you're firing a fully tested 122-millimetre Grad rocket from a fully tested rocket-launcher located 6.000 metres away from the target, there is a 50 per cent chance that the rocket will land within an ellipse which is 404 metres by 68 metres; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So essentially what you're saying is that both the FAB-100 modified air bomb launched from a modified rail launch system and the FAB-250 modified air bomb launched from a modified air -- rail launch system were a hell of a lot more accurate than the 120-millimetre Grad rocket when fired as a rocket.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There is an error here in the methodology. If you were listening to me carefully when I was talking before the break about probable deviations, you would have heard me say that in case of rocket projectiles we have a somewhat unusual phenomenon present. The reason is the reactive force and the influence of the wind. At shorter ranges there is a larger dispersion of hits in comparison with the dispersion along the direction when the distance is longer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last bit that he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, you are speaking very fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat from "At shorter ranges ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At shorter ranges, rocket projectiles had a bigger dispersion in comparison with longer ranges, whereas dispersion along a direction is less for bigger ranges and bigger for bigger ranges. Rocket projectiles such as Grad, they have a range of 21 kilometres, and the range in question of 6.000 -- or 6.000 metres is its initial phase for it. It's the short range. And as we can see from the table if we move downwards, you will see that at a distance of 8.000 metres the probable deviation is 173 metres, and along the direction it has increased to 45 metres. This is what I'm talking about. We did not choose an adequate comparison. When it comes to air bombs, the range of 6.000 metres is almost its ultimate range. I believe that according to our tables it can fly for 8.000 metres, 10.000 metres at the most, but that's a different part of its capabilities. This is for Grad the initial phase, hence big deviations, and that can be seen in the table as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But you've nevertheless claimed to this Trial Chamber, it's your expert evidence that at 6.000 metres both the FAB-100 and the FAB-250 are more accurate than the rocket when it's launched as a rocket; that's what you're asking this Trial Chamber to accept.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This kind of comparison in practical terms is impossible. We obtained our results based on a model which is also applied in these type of rockets. In other words, every projectile has its own characteristics, its mass, pressures, velocity, and so on and so forth. So all of that has an effect on its external ballistics characteristics. And according to the programme that can be applied here and that has been tested on similar projectiles, we arrived at a certain range of dispersion. I'm not saying that this is absolutely correct. It cannot be absolutely correct because we enter with certain assumptions which are customary or commonplace, because for us it was a completely new projectile. But it was customary that in the initial development stages that we base our estimates on assumptions. You don't need absolute figures for estimates, but I'm sure that when we did that, we did not make a big error.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when we go, please, to page 5, B/C/S page 5 in English, this is a point that you've alluded to earlier. But the Grad 122-millimetre rocket when it was used as a rocket and fired, presumably from a fully tested rocket-launcher, was not supposed to be used for distances under 5.000 metres; isn't that right? And I'd invite you to look at the portion under the table which says: "The use M-21-OF projectiles for distances up to 5 kilometres is possible in extraordinary cases and only in situations where there are no friendly troops in the direction of fire, since a significant amount of short rounds are possible, caused by a large disperse of the projectile at these ranges." I'm putting it to you, Mr. Poparic, that --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. What table is that? I cannot find my bearings in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Please look at -- under -- right in the centre of the page where you are, section 2, the first paragraph -- sorry, excuse me. I've given it to you the wrong -- it's right at the foot of the page. It's the last two lines right at the foot of the page in your version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you're done, we'll show you the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I don't see anything unusual here. I can explain why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page. I think it continues to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, we can go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So I'm putting it to you, Mr. Poparic, and I think you've essentially already acknowledged the point, that it would be highly irresponsible to use this particular rocket as a rocket for distances of under 5.000 metres; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Grad rocket projectile?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Grad 122-millimetre rocket projectile.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is very normal because -- let me explain why this was introduced. Grad is a rocket whose range is 21 kilometres. When it is fired at ranges up to 5.000 metres it has a larger dispersion. At shorter distances, it has larger dispersions because this is a characteristic not only of the Grad projectile but of all the other rocket projectiles. It is only logical that such a warning is given. This is not a ban; this is just a warning of an imminent danger. And in order to avoid short rounds and putting friendly troops in jeopardy, Grad is used from the rear and usually rockets are launched over friendly troops, hence the warning. We saw that dispersions are small and the same would apply in air bombs. I'm sorry that that part is redacted. We have provided all of those curves. And the same applies to air bombs where there's a large dispersion at a distance of 1.000 metres. There is nothing illogical here, either here or in what we came up with. Both is in line with the basic characteristics of those projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And this rocket, just to close out this point, we can agree it's designed and tested to be fired from a range of between 5 and 21 kilometres, it's an area weapon, and would you agree that it should be used for a situation such as destroying small vehicles in the open?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grad is a rocket for fire support. It is primarily used for shelling a larger area before an infantry attack is launched. Artillery support implies large-scale shelling of an area in order to suppress the enemy forces and allow an easier attack of infantry units. So the main purpose is to fire from the rear at larger distances. So this is just a formality, when it says 5.000 metres, because it never happens unless there is a very exceptional situation. But I don't see any connection with air bombs. We -- there's no comparison between the two. We're talking about major differences in the ranges of those two projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, you have touched on a very important point because earlier on you said - this is at page 57, line 1 - you were talking about a modified air bomb and you said: "This is practically a rocket, a rocketised projectile. We are saying that these are modified bombs, but actually it's a rocket." It's true, isn't it, that a modified air bomb and a rocket are totally different objects ballistically and in every way possible when it comes to launching them and determining where they're going to go; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. In ballistic terms this can be seen as the same type of projectile. In terms of appearance it deviates from the usual image we have of a rocket projectile. If a cover was put around the rocket engines, the term for that is capotage, which is a French term. It would look like a rocket projectile and everybody would say: Here you have it, a rocket projectile. In terms of its ballistic characteristics, it fully falls under the category of rocket projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the deviation, I repeat that I'm sorry that we don't have the diagram because I would be able to show you that there is the same characteristic of probable dispersions, both in Grad rockets as well as in air bombs. In ballistic terms they correspond to the characteristics of rocket projectiles and they have nothing in common with air bombs in ballistic terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, let's just take one issue, and that is the warhead. It's correct, isn't it, that the warhead on a rocket has the exactly same diameter as the rocket, whereas the warhead on a modified air bomb is a massive, great big air bomb, which is a much bigger diameter than the rocket; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If we take into account that there are four rocket engines in the biggest air bomb and the calibre of those is 122 millimetres, when this is distributed this would be the diameter of the warhead or somewhat bigger. But this doesn't change anything in its characteristics. The resistance may be a bit bigger or range may be somewhat smaller. However, when it comes to the function and ballistic characteristics, it still falls under the category of rocket projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've touched on the cross-sectional area of the two objects. It's true, isn't it, that a modified air bomb could be up to 3 and a half metres in length and with a breadth considerably greater than a Grad 122-millimetre rocket; that is to say both the length and breadth of a modified air bomb are greater than a rocket, giving rise to a much greater cross-sectional area and giving rise to greater interference from cross wind.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "width," did you mean the calibre or the cross-section? What did you mean? It was translated as "width" to me, whereas I believe that you meant diameter. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. The diameter and the length of any of the modified air bombs that you accept were fired by the VRS is much greater than the diameter and length of the 122-millimetre Grad rocket.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the calibre and the length are bigger, but that doesn't diminish the characteristics of the air bomb. It has nothing whatsoever to do with the Grad rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your report you've referred to the use of different kinds of launchers for the Grad rocket; however, they're all barrel launchers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand your question, sir. This is the interpretation that I have received. They would like you to repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The rockets described in your report were launched -- were designed and tested to be launched from barrels or tubes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you are asking me about the Grad rocket launcher, yes, we're talking about barrels, just like we are when Plamen and Oganj are referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the modified air bombs were launched from rails; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The modified air bombs with three and four rockets required absolutely synchronous ignition of those rockets; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely synchronised ignition does not exist; it's impossible to achieve. I would like to explain what requirements had to be satisfied. There had to be a delay of each engine within certain limits and those were milliseconds. And let me tell you how ignition can be delayed. When a rocket engine is ignited, there is a small element that we called a Schaefers head. It's a pyrotechnical mixture packed into a small ball where there is a thread, a wire thread, just like in a classical bulb, for example, and it is connected to a source of electrical energy. It ignites the pyrotechnical mass that in turn ignites the rocket. This is very strictly controlled and there shouldn't be a delay in ignition of more than a millisecond. And that delay can have absolutely no impact on the function of the trajectory of an aerial bomb. I could explain that better on the diagram that we saw about the pressure of the rocket engine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The modified air bombs required as close to possible synchronous ignition, whereas a rocket fired as a rocket is never fired synchronously with other rockets; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your term "absolutely synchronous ignition," this is a requirement on both a rocket as well as an air bomb. There is a justification for that and you mentioned it yourself. This has an impact on the stability of the multi-barrel launcher. There shouldn't be a large delay. That's why there should be a very small delay in the ignition of a rocket engine. The guarantee for a short delay is also the guarantee of the reliability of that rocket engine. This means that this will not result in a faulty ignition during the launch. This is the guarantee that we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, we're going to move on to another topic in a second, but can you answer the question that I asked you. The question was this: The modified air bombs required as close to possible synchronous ignition, whereas a rocket fired as a rocket is never fired synchronously with other rockets; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is partly true. It depends on the mode of launching. If we have a multi-barrel launcher, such as we have for Grad and Oganj, there are various possibilities of launching. You can launch one rocket and you can also issue an order to launch all the rockets. When we have a lot of rockets --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- then it happens -- shall I finish my explanation, please. Then it happens that we have a simultaneous launch of rockets from various parts of the launcher. For example, if a rocket was launched from the lower left barrel, then another rocket is fired from the upper right barrel in order to keep the balance. So that is also one kind of simultaneity. There is a programme, an algorithmic programme, how to launch rockets at the same time. It is true that air bombs are launched at the same time; however, their ignition is interconnected, which means that they are -- that all the three or all the four rockets are ignited at the same time. The possible delay in ignition is in the order of 1 millisecond and this doesn't have an impact on the function of that air bomb on its trajectory. If you could show me that diagram and to everybody in the courtroom, then I could make myself more clear and explain why this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I seek admission of the firing tables which is 65 ter 24036?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many pages does it have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we admit the cover page and the relevant page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I've shown several pages to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit those pages shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on to the question of the time taken to develop a new weapons system in the weapons industry in the former Yugoslavia prior to the conflict in Bosnia. Now, I believe that in your expert report which is the inconsistencies report, if we could turn, please, to page 76 in English and page 80 in B/C/S of the inconsistencies report which is 1D05600 - it does have a D number, D3644 - and in this paragraph you are discussing the question of fuel air bombs. Now, setting aside for a moment the entire debate about fuel air bombs, you appear to agree with Mr. Zecevic that developing a new weapons system would take around five to seven years in the former Yugoslavia. Do you agree with that basic assertion?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is information from practice. It is more or less true, but we mustn't -- we mustn't neglect that it says "complete." Here the idea of developing a fuel air bomb is discussed. That would be a new asset and we're talking about a typical duration to develop such an asset.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. The -- it's fair to say that your words "which is true" appear on the next page in English. Now, how long did it take to develop the modified air bombs systems used by the VRS to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know when the development started. The first use was in 1995 in Sarajevo. I believe it was on the 7th of April. So it could have taken up to three years. I must also add that this was not a completely new projectile. There is -- there was the propulsion group of a Russian manufacturer which was thoroughly tested and -- tested, which was very important. We had complete engines and complete air bombs. The task of the engineers was to make a synthesis of an air bomb and the propulsion --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which required aerodynamic calculations to determine the size of the fins. And there was also the problem of connecting the engine to the air bomb. In parallel, the launcher had to be developed. So I don't agree that five to seven years were required to develop such an asset because it was basically the integration of two well-tested products that were produced in series.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, that's exactly where I think we might have to seek your clarification. If you are integrating two well-tested products, welding them together, putting them onto a launch system which is itself new and untested and you are using this system with different weights of air bombs and with different numbers of rockets, it's absolutely vital that you should carry out exhaustive testing of each kind of air bomb and each configuration, depending on how many rockets you are attaching to it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a long and complex question so let me answer in stages. To complete such a system, based on my experience, it's realistic to expect six months to one year for all the calculations, for defining all parameters, for testing at ranges, for making firing tables, and so on. As for the launcher, that is a parallel process, and from the documents that were available to us, some of them were -- refer directly to launchers and some of them were made by the Hadzici maintenance centre which was used for all such assets in former Yugoslavia. And according to what I saw, the parts of existing artillery weapons were used, which again is not a totally new system. So there was -- there were existing supporting bipods and the launcher itself was the least of our problems. And we know that these launchers were tested. A year must have been enough to do all that. Up to one year, that's my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You'll certainly agree that the Vd and Vp for, for example, a FAB-250 would be different depending on whether it had three or four rockets welded to it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this was interpreted to me correctly because the engines are not welded but screwed on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for dispersion, range dispersion, in connection with these two models you mentioned, I agree that there must have been some difference but the difference cannot be great because in all rocket projectiles, including artillery projectiles, dispersion is always in correlation with the range. So expressed as percentages, they're always very similar. There can be a difference of 5 to 10 metres, but for such an asset this is not significant. There can be no drastic dispersion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll note for the record --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 4 and 5 on 76 page, it's rather confusing. Witness said there were lafets - I don't know how to translate it - that were well tested, and it was not problem and that it was our problem -- it was least problem. But lafets have been used as another element that was well tested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll note for the record that in the Vd and Vp data that you provided to the Trial Chamber in the table we were looking at earlier on, you did not distinguish between FAB-250s with three rockets compared to FAB-250s with four rockets, nor did you distinguish between FAB-100s with one rocket and FAB-100s with three rockets.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain why. I've already said that this is an analysis of some systems that are -- with which we were not completely acquainted. That's why we made a comparative analysis of all these systems, for us to enable to -- for us to be able to compare them. That's why we chose the range of 6.000 metres and that was the basis for our analysis. As for your assertion that there is a difference, well, some values are almost the same. There is dispersion -- range dispersion. It's too bad that we don't have the diagram which shows these values by range and by type of projectile.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we perhaps be shown the diagram upon which the witness relies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was redacted; that's why it's missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, we can probably bring up the relevant page later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd just like to just return to the question of the time for development of the new weapons system, and could I call up, please, 65 ter 25062. This is a statement of Djordje Djukic, who is described as assistant commander for logistics of the VRS, taken on the 4th February 1996. It appears to be taken by the RBiH MUP. It was provided to the ICTY by AID Sarajevo on the 29th of February, 1996. At the end of the first paragraph we see that this is a supplementary statement regarding the creation, use of, and decision-making on the use of a modified rocket system armed with aerial bombs. Now, I'd like to take you to the first words of the part under the heading "Supplementary Statement." And he says: "As far as I can recall, this method of using aircraft bombs that are launched by rocket engines was first mentioned approximately a year after the air force of Republika Srpska was forbidden to fly." Now, I want to put it to you - and I can give you evidence of this if you want - that it was in October 1992 that the Security Council prohibited -- passed a resolution prohibiting the flight of military aircraft over the air-space of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we go further on through this, I'd like to take you, it's the same page in both languages, further down where the witness says: "I know that the first systems used a single-rocket engine for propulsion and that this is what probably caused the launches to fail. After the rocket battery was built with two or three engines, the launches probably became more successful and in my judgement the modified system with four engines should be the most accurate." Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found this last part, but I accept that what you read out is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'll just read on. It says: "I think that the maximum range of this system is somewhere around 2 kilometres ..." If we could turn to the next page in B/C/S, please. It then says: "After Mladic" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It says there I believe, Mr. Witness: "After Mladic probably satisfied himself that the system was efficient, he issued an order to all the corps to proceed with building launchers. I know that Mladic ordered all corps of the Republika Srpska Army to build these launchers and he did so in contacts with corps commanders during meetings with commanders. The launchers were built in the corps." Now, first of all, there's a reference there to a maximum range of 2 kilometres. Now, that's somewhat at odds with --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood correctly he spoke about an air bomb with a single rocket engine which could correspond to that range. In the initial phase they only had one engine. We didn't see this type in Sarajevo except in one case at the Faculty of Transportation Sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'm going to put it to you that if the 122-millimetre Grad rocket cannot responsibly be used for less than 5.000 metres, then to attach it to an air bomb and to use it at a range of 2.000 metres is highly irregular, if not irresponsible.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, you didn't understand my explanation why Grad is not recommended. It can be used but it's not recommended. We saw that the dispersion of rocket projectiles at smaller ranges is greater than at longer ranges. Grad is a long-range asset and the 5.000-metre range is small for Grad. At such small ranges, it has great dispersion as you have shown, whereas an air bomb has a smaller range. 2 to 3 kilometres is a longer range for that kind of projectile. So we cannot compare an air bomb with Grad. That's the mistake. We cannot compare these two because they have totally different characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Furthermore, in -- according to this statement, Mladic ordered all the corps of the VRS to build these launchers. Now, it's certainly highly irregular for new complex launch systems for new projectiles to be built by the corps of the army, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the corps cannot have made them, you can be sure of that. I saw in the documentation that the corps were sending some assets such as the supporting bipods, gun carriages, to be used to make these new assets. The corps cannot make new weapons because they don't have the equipment requirement. A corps can always have faulty or defective assets that they send to the maintenance or repair centre, and they were indeed sent to Hadzici. There are also documents showing that air bombs were sent from the units to Pretis to be modified. I don't know how exactly it functioned and I don't know which assets they exactly had, but they had some assets and they sent part of those assets to be modified. The corps certainly was in no position to make a launcher because they have no way of doing that. A corps is a military unit. This can only be done in a factory or in a technical repair centre. The centre at Hadzici is an institution which could do that very well and successfully. After all, that's why it was founded in the first place, and it functioned like that for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in English, please, and to page 4 in B/C/S. And at the top of this page in B/C/S, Mr. Witness, it says: "In connection with the use of these rocket systems, I need to point out that I know that it was the corps commander who would propose their use and that it was General Mladic personally who would approve their use. On one occasion, I was present at a conversation between General Mladic and one of the corps commanders when Mladic, in a conversation with this corps commander of the Army of Republika Srpska, approved the use of this weapons system. I am sure that no one except General Mladic could approve the use of this system and that each single use was approved personally by Mladic." And previously we see a reference to fall of 1994. First of all, can I get your confirmation that it is not usually the role of a general in the army to approve a new weapons system for use?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this question is very precise. It says here that General Mladic approved the use of an air bomb, which means that the bomb was in a unit. Somebody else must have checked the bombs, not General Mladic, it is for sure. And it is not unusual that General Mladic demands that he be the one to approve the use of these bombs. That's not unusual in an army because assets of great value, or rather, the use of such assets is often approved by high command. An asset worth 200.000 to $300.000 cannot be subject to decisions of a lower-ranking commander. A higher level decides about the use of such assets, and that's customary in an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Poparic, earlier on I ready to you a sentence which said: "After Mladic probably satisfied himself that the system was efficient, he issued an order to all the corps to proceed with building launchers." That suggests, doesn't it, that it was General Mladic who approved the use of this brand new improvised weapons system.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is a difference in your approach. In the JNA - I'll start like that and then return to this sentence - the practice was that the decision of the development of an asset was taken by the tactical bearer, such as the artillery administration, for example. They decided what they needed for the strategic tasks and they would make a request with the party in charge for something like that to be developed. I don't know how it was organised in the VRS, but we see here that Mladic ordered the development of such air bombs. And he was in a position to do unless there was a specific organ in the VRS, which I don't know. But in any case that was not outside his remit. But he didn't approve. He just ordered something like that to be developed for the VRS because he was able to see for himself that these were efficient and useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In any event I want to return to the question of the time taken to use the weapons system. If we agree that the no-fly zone was ordered in Bosnia on 9th of October, 1992, and if according to this witness the first mention of modified air bombs was a year later, which would be October 1993 at the earliest, then would you agree with me that this new weapons system was certainly brought into use in a much, much shorter time-frame than the customary five to seven years?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must intervene. I have a remark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be exactly related to the witness. In 1993 it was mentioned and in the fall of 1994 the engines were first procured. You cannot delude the witness with your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I think the question is fair enough and the witness should be able to answer the question. Yes, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've already answered that question and I'll repeat it once again. These modified air bombs were not a completely new asset. There are two very important key elements, the warhead which was the air bomb and also the rocket engines, the propulsion Russian-manufactured, imported. And this did not imply the development of a completely new weapon that would be included in this group of the development of new weapons that requires five or seven years of research and development. My assessment was that a weapon of such complexity could have been made in a period from sixth months to one year, and I claim that with full responsibility because I worked on such matters for many years. I'd like to note another thing. In peace time development was regulated by a set of rules, UPRF2. All stages were defined there and all the tasks that had to be carried out before a weapon would be introduced, starting with the very beginning of development and then moving on to who decides that this weapon should be included in the weaponry of the army. Also, this rule book had a part that regulated the development of weapons in war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It allowed certain stages to be skipped because of the extraordinary circumstances involved. So I don't see anything unusual about that; namely, that in my estimate the development could have lasted from six months to one year and that it would prove to be a good thing, as was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Have you ever seen contemporaneous firing tables for any of the modified air bomb systems? Or have you, during your long career at the technical test centre in Belgrade from 1991 to 2007, seen comprehensive test data for these modified air bomb systems?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally at the time was not working on that, but I do know that there were some firing tables. That was a colleague of mine who worked on that and these tables certainly did exist. Probably they could be obtained if the appropriate authorities were asked for that. May I remind you of something? The Army of Yugoslavia introduced the Koseva system in its own weapons, very similar to this system. As a matter of fact, it was even presented at an exhibition partner in 2000 something. I cannot recall the exact year. It was even offered for sale.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I -- the document you were hoping to see, Mr. Poparic, is available as a 65 ter number 25082, if we could look at that, please. In the meantime, can you just confirm that you have never seen with your own eyes contemporaneous firing tables or contemporaneous test data for any of these modified air bomb systems; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the tables but I don't know exactly what year it was. I saw it on the man's desk. I wasn't interested. I could not confirm the year, whether it was 1995 or later, but I know that the tables do exist. Whose they were and who made them, I do not know. What was the second part of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Contemporaneous test data?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't involved in this kind of work so I don't have contemporaneous test data, which is not to say that this does not exist if I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, if you do come across those firing tables, I'm sure the Trial Chamber would be happy to receive them. If you could look at the table in front of you and make whatever observations you would wish to make to the Trial Chamber about this table, I believe this is the one you indicated you wanted to look at.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Which table did you want to see, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I spoke about diagrams where you can see the dispersion at the beginning of the trajectory and that it's bigger than and then it decreases, and also probable dispersion according to direction. It's probably the other way around -- well, never mind. I think we showed that with the table for Grad, and that table clearly shows that dispersion in terms of range increases with the increase of range; and then when range is increased -- well, it's quite clear from that table and I think that suffices for the time being. Let us not torment ourselves with that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to move on to the Markale 2 incident which is subsequentially the first issue addressed in your report. First of all, let's sort out a French language issue. Could I call up, please, page 113 B/C/S, page 112 English of your inconsistencies report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before you move away from this document, this is the part of the redacted report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, this is a part of -- which has been redacted from the inconsistencies report of this witness, which is D3644.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the witness referred to some graph which seems to appear at the end of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I'll defer to you on that one. I wasn't sure which graph it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last page of this one, excerpt, this 65 ter number. Did you mean this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I meant -- that's one of the examples. You see this here, the red line, it shows the deviation in terms of range depending on the range. The ranges are down there and the blue line is deviation in terms of direction. Here we can see that at the beginning of the trajectory it's bigger and then it decreases, and that is quite evident from the Grad table. That is a joint characteristic of all rocket projectiles. That's the way it is with each and every rocket projectile. However, the situation is different as far as artillery is concerned. This is just to show it in visual terms, what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to you then. Please continue, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We have time I think to sort out one French language issue. It's page 112 in English, page 113 in B/C/S of D3644. Do you speak French, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I used to but it's been a while now that I haven't. I do understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we please look at footnote 211, and in that footnote you are suggesting -- we need footnote 211 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask whether this diagram had been tendered? If it could be admitted, then I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We've no objection to the admission of those pages which had been redacted from the inconsistencies report. It appears that the parties, I believe, have no objection to the admission of those pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At least to understand what the -- part of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Five pages or those two pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I have no objection to the admission of the five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6348, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in that footnote you say: "In the video material the French sapper measuring the azimuth is heard saying 2.100 mils." We're now going to play that video, which is P1450, from 5 minutes and 40 seconds to 5 minutes and 50 seconds, and we'll just listen to what the French sapper is actually saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, subject to any correction by the interpretation booths, I believe that we have just heard the soldier say in French "2.800 mils."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps, Judge Lattanzi, if she wishes, can correct me on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She confirms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, do you accept that you were mistaken when you said that the French sapper said 2.100 mils?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Absolutely correct. I can explain the nature of this error. I see now that it's an error. I hadn't seen it before that. The first time when we listened to this text, in the French language they speak very fast and I asked other people who know French -- everybody heard "2.100," and that's when I wrote that down but we weren't sure of that. And then when a witness was here it was played twice back to check that and it was 2.800. I accept that it is 2.800 and that is an accidental error that remained from the previous time. We didn't manage to correct it. So 2.800, that would be, well, a bit less than 160 degrees, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the French report, which is P2114, they have put down 2.850 mils at several locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I believe we can break here for today, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll hear another witness's evidence tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We've asked to interrupt the testimony of this witness for Mr. Kecmanovic who has to leave. So if we could start him at 9.00 and then resume with his witness as soon as his testimony is concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've had lengthy discussions with Mr. Robinson on this, many of which were triggered by the length of time taken by Mr. Karadzic in contrast to the earlier estimates. The problem is that Mr. Gaynor is required to leave tomorrow. We need him to finish the cross-examination. My concern is that based on the accused's use of time in the past, if we commence with Mr. Kecmanovic's evidence tomorrow, the accused is undisciplined enough, as he's indicated, to exhaust the full day in either direct or re-direct examination and Mr. Gaynor will not have an opportunity to complete the cross. I think it's a far safer course to allow him to complete. I don't know how much time he has, but it's in the area of one hour, and that will still leave us more than adequate time, given the estimates, which at this time will have to be roughly complied with to fulfil both objectives and allow the proceeding to conclude in an appropriate fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much time was allotted for the cross-examination of Mr. Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two hours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it that your case is -- Mr. Gaynor is not needed during the re-examination of Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. This is one of the reasons I had lengthy discussions with Mr. Robinson. We did not want to find ourselves in this position. This is yet another compromise and accommodation by the Prosecution, contrary to our intentions, our hopes, and our best efforts, all of which resulted from lavish uses of time contrary to previous estimates by the accused. So we are in that position and we -- you know, we don't like to find ourselves in a position where Mr. Gaynor isn't available for the entirety of the examination for obvious reasons. But that was a compromise we were willing to make with considerable discomfort. But we certainly aren't willing to go any farther than that. We need to have Mr. Gaynor complete the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see much difficulty with what Mr. Tieger suggests now. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Gaynor can be trusted to keep to the estimate probably better than Dr. Karadzic. So if we can count on there being only one hour of cross-examination, then I think we can all be accommodated by that. So we can go ahead and conclude the cross-examination at 9.00, and then we'll have Mr. Kecmanovic immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's very well. By 9.00 you probably mean 10.00, I think. Yes, that concludes my part of the cross-examination. Ms. Edgerton will have separate cross-examination on the sniping report but this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After Kecmanovic's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your co-operation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't want to feel as if I'm being done a favour. How is -- how am I being satisfied if it's Mr. Gaynor who's supposed to leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is scheduling is up to the Defence. Those schedules are based on their own estimates. We've adhered to our own estimates. If Mr. Kecmanovic is in a position that creates a problem for Defence scheduling, it's entirely the product of Mr. Karadzic's use of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 31st day of May, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
